messages.subject: New version of AHMbook R package
messages.subject_clean: New version of AHMbook R package
messages.body_plain:
Applied Hierarchical Modeling in Ecology is the book about unmarked. It comes with an R package, AHMbook, with lots of functions to complement unmarked.

We have just wrapped up a new version of the AHMbook package, v. 0.1.1. Details of changes are below.

The new version depends on other packages, which you can install or update with

install.packages(c("unmarked", "plotrix", "sp", "raster", "RandomFields", "coda"))

If you have all those installed and you are running R 3.3.x, you can install the new package with

install.packages("AHMbook", repos = "http://mikemeredith.net/R")

The same URL <http://mikemeredith.net/R/> will get you to a page where you can download the source or binaries for manual installation.

New in AHMbook version 0.1.1
Full help pages for all functions.
New names: plot.Nmix.resi -> plot_Nmix_resi and image.scale -> image_scale, to prevent clashes with R's 'plot' and 'image' generic functions.
Fewer dependencies, and all checked when you load AHMbook: no more "there is no package called xxx" when you try to run a function.
Changes to the "histograms" of counts, using transparent colours when two counts are plotted together.
The dragonfly data have been tidied up; do data(dragonfly) before use.
New functions for AHM Volume 2: simDynocc and simDCM.
The 'jay' dataset has migrated to 'unmarked' package.
Fixed: bugs involving 'logit'.
Fixed: data.fn() now corresponds to the code in section 4.3.
Fixed: simHDSg("point", ...), sim.spatialDS() and sim.spatialHDS() now work.
Fixed: plotting functions now restore the settings of the graphics window on exit.
Note: simComm("counts",...), simHDStr("point",...), and simHDSopen("point",...) give slightly different results even with the same seed; all the other simulations give the same values as before when set.seed() is used.
Thanks to Marc for help with the documentation and to Andy for finding some missing code.

messages.body_plain:
Does it fit if you remove the starting values? Perhaps also try "se = FALSE" when you create the p.null model and then coef(p.null) to generate starting values for models with covariates.

Your starting values for lambda (0), phi (0), and sigma (5) should be based on whatever you think is a reasonable expectation, and I see a couple problems with the numbers you chose.

For lambda, I believe a starting value of 0.0 will create an error because it's on log scale. So start with a much larger number here (something like 2 or 4 perhaps) as it appears that your abundances are generally >1.

For phi you will also want a higher starting value as this is on logit scale which implies availability ~ 0.5. If you feel that your birds are generally available (temporary emigration is low) across repeated visits then values up to ~4 might be more realistic.

For sigma I typically see values in the 3-5 range with forest birds so your start of 5.0 seems reasonable.

Hope this helps!

Jay

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] How to write the instruction for model psi(.) p(t) in unmarked?
messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] How to write the instruction for model psi(.) p(t) in unmarked?
messages.body_plain:
A short answer is occu(~ t ~ 1, data = mariposa).

A longer answer is a complete working example:

> # Temporal detection probability example
>
> # Set model parameters
>   nSites <- 100
>   nVisits = 5
>   # Probability of presence at a site
>   psi <- 0.6
>   # Detection probability is linear in logit over visit number
>   a <- 0
>   b <- 0.5
>   logitp <- a + b*c(1:nVisits)
>   p <- 1 - 1/(1+exp(logitp))
>
> # Generate data
>   trueState <- rbinom(nSites,1,psi)
>   y <- trueState*matrix(c(rbinom(nSites,1,p[1]),
>          rbinom(nSites,1,p[2]),
>          rbinom(nSites,1,p[3]),
>          rbinom(nSites,1,p[4]),
>          rbinom(nSites,1,p[5])), nrow=nSites, ncol=nVisits, byrow=FALSE)
>   t <- matrix(rep(1:nVisits,nSites), nrow=nSites, ncol=nVisits, byrow=TRUE)
>   library(unmarked)
>   umf <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y=y, obsCovs=list(t=t))
>
> # Run analysis
>   occu(~ t ~ 1, umf)

A better answer is to first think about why and then how the detection probabilities might change in time.  Is some bait going stale over time?  Are visits not independent?  Is the critter learning over time? etc.  Then try a plausible model form for the change in detection probabilities.

Jim

FYI I and my colleagues have found that for most birds, as long as you implement basic field survey strategies to maximize consistency of detections (survey in early morning when activity is highest, do surveys well within breeding season after spring migration and before late summer redistributions, don't survey in bad weather, etc) that availability is generally very high. What appears to end up happening is that the gdistsamp model has trouble distinguishing phi and detection probability for data sparse species. Because of this we've settled on distsamp as the preferred alternative for several recent analyses.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Everyone!

Sorry if these are really basic questions (and probably not solely related to unmarked), but I have  been stuck with linearComb() and could not find the answers to my questions in the FAQ, the vignette or here (although I am very sorry if it is already covered somewhere).
I am using pcount() for the estimation of abundance and detection of single season data of different species (one model per species) with M = 55 sites and J = 8 visits (all sites had 8 visits). My obsCovs (time after sunrise, day of year, number of other individuals present) were scaled using the scale() function, my SiteCovs (proportional area of open, forest and urban area at each site) are not scaled but just devided by 100 (eg. 40,20,20 for 40% open, 20% forest and urban habitat). Except for cases where a site only consists of 1 habitat, they never sum up to 100% because of other habitats  and to avoid collinearity.
My problem is the interpretation and transformation of estimates when my best model includes quadratic terms in the state and/or det process.

Those are the estimates I get for one of my species:
StateEstimates:
     (Intercept)      Forest_Area I(Forest_Area^2)
       -1.401179         8.266376        -5.356210

DetEstimates
   (Intercept)      StartTime I(StartTime^2)
    -1.2629669     -1.0653560     -0.8903796

My Questions are:
1.) due to the horrendous estimates, I assume backTransform() is not applicable to my type = "state" estimates (makes sence), but how can I backtransform them manually, ?
2.) what will backTransform(linearComb(BestModel, coefficients =  DetEstimates)) exactly output, what do the estimated numbers say? Mean det / abundance per site?
3.) let's suppose, I want to plot the influence of StartTime on the Detection: I know I have to create a matrix specifying values for each of the coefficients and calculate each linearComb(), but what do i put in for these?
As I specified StartTime in minutes after sunrise, will I just use "60" for the estimate 1 hour after sunrise, or do I have to use the a transformed version of this number? What can I use for the squared Starttime? simply the sqrt(StartTime) (or the transformed version)?

With writing, I realised how basic these questions must have to be for some of you. however, for me they are not, so I hope you don't mind me asking them here.
Thx for your time and, hopefully, answers to my questions, Christian

This is the model where (1-epsilon)=gamma so that occupancy in season t+1 does not depend on occupancy in the previous season. Some models can be fit using separate occupancy models for each season, but then you can't share information about p across seasons.

Thanks

Carl Schwarz

Yes.  Each year has a separate parameter for psi (or one could fit some function that relates the psi values among years).  It's as if there's a new random set of sites for each year.  (Offhand I don't know if the AIC values could be directly compared between occu models and colext models. I understand that pooling data gets one more precise estimates (but only if one can assume rather than just willing to assume that there's a common detection probability).

Jim

Here is my sample code to fit a random occupancy model using the occu() function.  The test data is a 3 seasons of 2 visits/season as indicated by the visits vector in the code. The code assumes that a row.name <http://row.name> is available for the input history -- it fails if there is no row name, so you should add a simple row.name <http://row.name> such as the site id or 1:nsites.

library(unmarked)

history <-read.csv('test-random.csv',  header=TRUE, as.is <http://as.is>=TRUE, row.names=1)
head(history)

# We need to split the data into separate sets of sites for each season
# and put all NA's before and after the season of interest
# COnsider a study with 3 seasons and 2 visits/season
# The history 101101 is broken into 3 pseudo-histories
#     10....
#     ..11..
#     ....01
# Then to allow a separate psi for each season, you add a site covariate to give
#   SiteCov  History
#     T1     10....
#     T2     ..11..
#     T3     ....01
# and then fit the model with  psi~SiteCov

visits <- c(2,2,2)  # 3 seasons with 2 visits per season
start.visit <- cumsum(c(0,visits[-length(visits)]))+1 # when does season start
end.visit   <- cumsum(visits)  # when does season end

rev.history <- NULL # revised history that isolates each season with NA in front and after the season's data
for(i in 1:length(visits)){
   season.history <- cbind(matrix(NA,nrow=nrow(history),ncol=max(0,start.visit[i]-1)),
                           history[, start.visit[i]:end.visit[i]],
                           matrix(NA,nrow=nrow(history),ncol=max(0,end.visit[length(end.visit)]-end.visit[i])))
   row.names(season.history) <- paste("SEAS.", formatC(i, digits=2, flag='0'),'.',row.names(season.history),sep="")
   names(season.history) <- names(history)  # fix up the visit names
   rev.history<- rbind(rev.history,season.history)
}

# create a site covariate that reflects the different seasons for the rev.history
rev.history.site.cov <- data.frame(Season=rep(paste("SEAS.", formatC(1:length(visits), digits=2, flag='0'),sep=""), each=nrow(history)))

#   SiteCov  History
#     T1     10....

rev.history <- NULL # revised history that isolates each season with NA in front and after the season's data
for(i in 1:length(visits)){
   season.history <- cbind(matrix(NA,nrow=nrow(history),ncol=max(0,start.visit[i]-1)),
                           history[, start.visit[i]:end.visit[i]],
                           matrix(NA,nrow=nrow(history),ncol=max(0,end.visit[length(end.visit)]-end.visit[i])))
   row.names(season.history) <- paste("SEAS.", formatC(i, digits=2, flag='0'),'.',row.names(season.history),sep="")
   names(season.history) <- names(history)  # fix up the visit names
   rev.history<- rbind(rev.history,season.history)
}

# create a site covariate that reflects the different seasons for the rev.history
rev.history.site.cov <- data.frame(Season=rep(paste("SEAS.", formatC(1:length(visits), digits=2, flag='0'),sep=""), each=nrow(history)))
rev.history.site.cov$Time <- rep(1:length(visits), each=nrow(history))

Seasons <- matrix( rep(c("T1","T2","T3"),each=2), nrow=nrow(rev.history), ncol=ncol(rev.history), byrow=TRUE)

occ.UMF <- unmarkedFrameOccu(
  y = rev.history,
  obsCovs=list(Season=Seasons),
  siteCovs=rev.history.site.cov)
occ.UMF
summary(occ.UMF)
plot(occ.UMF, panels=1)

mod

psi.pred.cov <- data.frame(Season=unique(rev.history.site.cov$Season))

cbind(psi.pred.cov, psi.pred)

p.pred.cov <- data.frame(one=1)
p.pred <- predict(mod, type="det", newdata=p.pred.cov)
cbind(p.pred.cov, p.pred)

mod

cbind(psi.pred.cov, psi.pred)

p.pred <- predict(mod, type="det", newdata=p.pred.cov)
cbind(p.pred.cov, p.pred)

# Now to fit a model for random occupancy with a time trend across seasons but a common p across all seasons
mod2 <- occu( ~1 ~Time, data=occ.UMF)

mod2

psi.pred.cov <- data.frame(Time=1:length(visits))
psi.pred     <- predict(mod2, type="state", newdata=psi.pred.cov)
cbind(psi.pred.cov, psi.pred)

p.pred.cov <- data.frame(one=1)
p.pred <- predict(mod2, type="det", newdata=p.pred.cov)
cbind(p.pred.cov, p.pred)

mod3

psi.pred.cov <- data.frame(Time=1:length(visits))
psi.pred     <- predict(mod3, type="state", newdata=psi.pred.cov)
cbind(psi.pred.cov, psi.pred)

p.pred.cov <- data.frame(Season=c("T1","T2","T3"))
p.pred <- predict(mod3, type="det", newdata=p.pred.cov)
cbind(p.pred.cov, p.pred)
